judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 2122, which would have stopped Arizona easing the work rule attached to food assistance. The state could not have sought, accepted or renewed any waiver of the work requirement for able-bodied adults without dependants unless federal law required it or state law allowed it. It also could not have used the state's own option to exempt anyone. The Arizona House passed it 33-27, and the Governor vetoed it.

The Department of Economic Security would have had to ask the federal government for permission to exclude it, and to keep asking every year until permission was granted. Soda was defined as a fizzy drink with more than one gram of added sugar or any artificial sweetener. The Arizona House passed it 32-27, and the Governor vetoed it.

The Arizona Senate passed it 17-13, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 2202, which would have let farmers move an old pumping right onto new ground. A grandfathered irrigation right lets land keep drawing groundwater because it was farmed before the area came under limits. Inside the newer management areas, the holder could have irrigated land never irrigated before, if it sits next to a farm unit that was, and if the total water drawn did not rise. The Arizona House passed it 32-27, and the Governor vetoed it.

The Arizona Senate passed it 16-14, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 2221, which would have stopped cities cutting police budgets. A city could not have set a police budget below the previous year's. A city that did cut would have kept its state-shared money only in listed situations, such as having too little money, cutting every other department by as much or more, or having no population growth. The Arizona Senate passed it 16-13, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 2222, which would have required warning before a public body settles a case. The Attorney General would have had to send the proposed terms to the leaders of both chambers at least 30 days beforehand. Cities and counties would have had to send theirs to the Governor, both chambers and the Attorney General at least 90 days beforehand. The Arizona Senate passed it 17-12, and the Governor vetoed it.

Before the commission, its staff or its lobbyists argued for or against a bill or a rule, the commission would have had to take a majority vote at a publicly noticed meeting and publish its position. The Attorney General could have investigated a failure to do so. The Arizona Senate passed it 17-12, and the Governor vetoed it.

Where a parent asked in writing between May 1 and August 15, the home school district would have had to start the evaluation, or refuse in writing, within 15 calendar days. The Arizona House passed it 33-26, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 2450, which would have tied how long unemployment benefits last to the jobless rate. The schedule started at 12 weeks while unemployment is 5 percent or less. It rose in steps as the rate rose, reaching 24 weeks once unemployment passed 7.5 percent. The rate for the previous quarter would have set the length. The Arizona House passed it 32-26, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 2527, which would have made it harder to close a power plant. The Corporation Commission could not have approved retiring a generating plant unless a new plant of equal or greater output was already available. The commission would have had to favor sources that can be switched on to order, and to plan for at least 5 percent more of that kind of power between 2025 and 2030. The Arizona House passed it 33-27, and the Governor vetoed it.

The bill set out how such a designation would be made and how long it would run. The Arizona Senate passed it 16-12, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 2788, which would have made electricity companies show their long-term plan. An electric utility would have had to file a resource plan with the Corporation Commission for review and approval at least every three years. The plan would have had to project demand 15 years ahead under low, medium and high growth, and list every plant it relies on and every one due to retire. The Arizona House passed it 31-28, and the Governor vetoed it.

A claimant would have had to take at least five job search actions each week and report them weekly. An existing requirement to search in a systematic way would have been removed. The department would also have cross-checked claims against other data. The Arizona House passed it 32-23, and the Governor vetoed it.

The Arizona House passed it 31-23, and the Governor vetoed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 1310, which would have raised the penalty for filing a fake claim against someone's property. Knowingly filing a false document that claims an interest in, or a lien on, land or a building would have become a class 4 felony. It is a class 1 misdemeanor now. The Arizona House passed it 34-23, and the Governor vetoed it.
